name: Xala Reef (Costalegre artificial surf reef)
place: Xala development, Costalegre coast, Jalisco (between Puerto Vallarta and Manzanillo)
year: Unclear/phased: boulder surf break reported built by April 2025 [R3][R4]; Raised Water Research calls it 'newly completed' and, in its announcement of 31 March 2026, billed a reveal event for 16 April 2026 [R1]
type: Rock/boulder reef — 3,000 truckloads of quarried boulders, not geotextile sand tubes [R3][R4]
purpose: Dual: (1) private members'-only high-performance surf break for Xala's owners/guests; (2) coastal protection/beach restoration, engineered to 'restore the beach, not flatten it' [R3][R4][R5]
size: Not disclosed — no length, width, crest depth, or fill volume found in any source this sweep [R1][R3][R4][R5] Shape/3D model: none, trace not possible (07_scale/shapes/mexico-reef-2026-unnamed/HANDOFF.md): no image shows the structure and no dimensions or coordinates exist; the 160 x 80 m 'analogy envelope' in 07_scale/reefs/ and Gemini's ~140 x 75 m are unsourced and not used. The card therefore has no model numbers to match (statement about this project's own files, 07_scale/shapes/mexico-reef-2026-unnamed/HANDOFF.md).
cost: Not disclosed for the reef specifically [R3][R5]
financed_by: Xala development by Activos Turísticos de México (ACTUR), led by Ricardo Santa Cruz and Jerónimo Bremer [R3]; Richard Gere is a co-founder/backer [R3][R4]; Six Senses (IHG) will operate the resort hotel [R3][R5]. No source itemizes who specifically paid for the reef construction [R3][R4][R5]
motivation: Positioned as part of a 'regenerative,' low-density luxury development contrasted with conventional Mexican coastal resorts; developer Ricardo Santa Cruz frames the project around ecological restraint over density and a buyer base (largely Californian tech-wealth) that doesn't want a conventional resort [R3][R4]
designer: Simon Brandi Mortensen, Principal Coastal Engineer and Managing Director, DHI Seaport (MSc Coastal Engineering, TU Denmark; 19 years in coastal projects; designer of Australia's Palm Beach Reef) [R1][R6]
status_now: Described as complete ('newly completed') in Raised Water Research's announcement of 31 March 2026 [R1] (the source's framing, not a verified fact); that announcement billed a reveal at a California Surf Club event in Redondo Beach, CA, for 16 April 2026 [R1][R9]; no source seen reports that the event took place. Access is private/limited — Xala caps built units at 93 against an approved 4,500 [R1][R3][R4] Audit 2026-10-10: the earlier wording 'publicly unveiled 16 April 2026' was removed because it is not supported as a past event: R1 is an announcement posted 2026-03-31 that bills the reveal for 16 April 2026; no source seen reports that it took place, and 'complete and operational' is R1's framing, not a verified fact. (The shape HANDOFF carried the same wording; corrected in the citations audit of 2026-10-10.)
hover_text: A private, members'-only rock/boulder surf reef (3,000 truckloads of quarried boulders) built inside the Xala luxury resort development on Mexico's Costalegre coast, Jalisco; cost and exact build date undisclosed, announced 31 March 2026 with a public reveal billed for 16 April 2026 [R1] — too new for any independent outcome data to exist yet [R1][R3][R4].
design_as_planned: No detailed design brief (target wave height, period, break type, or beach-width promise) was found in the sources listed in References (negative finding of this card). Documented: quarried rock/boulder construction (3,000 truckloads), not geotextile sand-filled tubes [R3][R4], consistent with designer Simon Mortensen's stated philosophy that geotextile reefs suffer from bags 'breaking, shifting or sinking' with removal costs sometimes exceeding placement costs, whereas rock is 'natural and provides many small crevasses for marine habitat' [R12]. Stated intent: coastal protection/beach nourishment combined with a 'consistently great wave,' explicitly contrasted with reef designs that would 'flatten' rather than 'restore' the beach [R3][R4][R5]. No public engineering report, EIS, or design paper was located in this card's searches (negative finding).
as_built_vs_design: Not enough independent material was found (negative finding of this card) to compare as-designed vs as-built — no construction-progress reporting, as-built drawings, or named contractor were located. The only construction detail available (3,000 truckloads of quarry boulders) is presented in press coverage as the finished description, not a revised design target [R3][R4]. A roughly one-year gap between the reef being described as part of Xala's built amenities (April 2025 [R3][R4]) and Raised Water Research's 'newly completed'/unveiling framing (March–April 2026 [R1]) is unresolved in sources found — possibly phased construction, or the reef was substantially built by 2025 and only formally unveiled in 2026.
outcome: No independent surf report, wave-height measurement, or session footage description was found; Raised Water Research withheld even the reef's exact location until the reveal event billed for 16 April 2026 and promised 'never-before-seen footage,' implying essentially no public track record as of its 31 March 2026 announcement [R1]. Coastal-protection performance (before/after beach-profile or erosion data) is not measured/reported in any source found (negative finding of this card). Ecology is not reported for the reef structure itself, though the wider Xala site includes a leatherback/Olive Ridley/green sea-turtle sanctuary and Ramsar-listed estuaries as separate conservation features [R5][R10]. Access/longevity/damage-event data does not yet exist given that the reef was only announced in March-April 2026 [R1]; no source was found stating otherwise (negative finding of this card).
why_worked_or_failed: No outcome data was found to assess this directly (negative finding of this card). The only available engineering signal is designer pedigree: Simon Mortensen led the design of Australia's Palm Beach Reef (Gold Coast; design 2013–2014, construction April–September 2019 [R6][R7]; ~$18.2M AUD/~$12.5M USD, financed by the City of Gold Coast; 4–8 tonne rock boulders plus 470,000 m³ of beach-nourishment sand), which Raised Water Research assesses as a design success — 'the reef appears to be a success,' producing a consistent ~60 m right-hander and a shorter left in bigger swell [R7]. This is background on the designer's method only, not evidence about Xala's own performance — no source directly ties Palm Beach's outcome data to the Xala build. Decision: verdict 'n-a' was assigned by the dossier agent (verified_on 2026-09-24) because the reef is too new and no performance data exist [R1]; it is not a judgement of success or failure.
unexpected_results: Nothing Xala-specific was found in the sources listed in References (negative finding of this card) (no litigation, safety incidents, fishing pressure, rip currents, or tourism-surge reporting). One indirect signal: an unrelated online repost of the Hollywood Reporter piece on a political/finance forum drew at least one favorable outside comment calling the whole project 'a neat idea/project,' but this concerns the development in general, not the reef, and is a single anonymous forum post [R4].
could_be_better: No source listed in References offers a critique of the Xala reef specifically (negative finding of this card) (too new; no engineering post-mortem or surfer complaint thread was found). Generic rock-reef trade-off to watch for once surf reports exist: rock-bottom reefs (versus sand-bottom breaks) have drawn 'harder surface' complaints at other sites such as Palm Beach Reef (no source for this complaint is held in the Palm Beach card either, (unsourced)) — flagged here only as a general risk category, not a documented Xala complaint. No author/expert or surfer view was found for Xala specifically (negative finding); the site's private/members-only access model [R3][R4] may itself suppress independent public reviews for some time (the card author's inference).
relevance_to_israel: Tide range and local wave climate at the Xala/Costalegre site were not found in this card's searches. What transfers conceptually, independent of Xala's own unverified outcome (all items are the card author's inferences): (1) Material choice precedent — the designer's shift toward quarried rock/boulder construction [R3][R12] (also used at Palm Beach Reef, 4–8 t boulders [R7]) rather than geotextile sand-filled tubes is directly comparable to the geotube-vs-rock materials question already live in this project's Israel dossiers (e.g. Ashkelon's 2018 geotube) — a rock-reef alternative is one materials option Israeli planners could weigh against documented geotube failure modes (undersized tubes, sand burial). (2) Governance-model contrast — Xala's reef is privately financed and privately accessed (members-only resort [R3][R4][R5]), unlike Israel's public-agency-funded structures (e.g. Ashkelon, Michmoret), a useful contrast case for 'who pays / who gets access' framing, though not a coastal-engineering transfer.

reviews.quote_or_summary: Profile of the whole Xala project including the reef: 'a private high-performance surf break, courtesy of an artificial reef constructed with 3,000 truckloads of boulders from a nearby quarry... engineered to restore the beach, not flatten it.'
"Most are from California, a big tech contingent. They don't want Mom and Dad's country club resort. They want something real."

reviews.role: marine conservationist, Sierra a Mar co-founder
reviews.quote_or_summary: On coastal restoration philosophy generally: "Imagine having clean water, clean air and happy communities around you that don't hate you because you ruined the place. That has got to be the ultimate amenity."
On the project's social mission: "Our role is to awaken our communities' inner power to regenerate themselves."

reviews.role: founder of Raised Water Research (industry trade press)
reviews.quote_or_summary: Author of the reef-unveiling announcement, framing it as designer-pedigree news; unveiling event billed as a 'fireside conversation' with designer Simon Brandi Mortensen covering reef science and 'the future of reef projects along the California coast.'
Reacting to the wider Xala coverage (not reef-specific): calls the project "a neat idea/project."
